# Playbook for Sonar Picket

## Hiding Strategy
When the hide stage arrives, place yourself in a cell that balances predictability against centrality. Avoid extremes (1 or 9) in early rounds. Vary your position across rounds to prevent pattern exploitation. In early rounds, cells 3-7 are safe; as you gather data on opponent patterns, adjust based on what you observe in their notes and firing behavior.

## Station Notes
Use notes to signal genuine strategic intent without overcommitting. Avoid grandiose statements about "disciplined endgame strategy"—you don't know what the endgame will look like. Keep notes brief and honest about your actual constraints and willingness to collaborate. If you have established a mutual escort arrangement with another boat, confirm it explicitly in your note to reinforce the signal and lock in the coordination for the next round.

## Standing Order Compliance
When required to fire at the next live station in rotation, do so. Do not deviate from standing orders without compelling evidence that deviation benefits you more than compliance costs you.

## Fire Placement
When firing at an assigned target, choose your fire cell based on available information about their patterns or notes. In early rounds with no information, pick a moderate cell (4-6) rather than extremes. As the game progresses and you gather data from others' hiding patterns, adjust accordingly. Do not mirror your own hiding cell—this is predictable and wastes the independence of your two strategic choices.

## Claim Honesty
Always report the true result the office gives you. False claims create no long-term advantage in a short game and damage your credibility if discovered. The scoring from a single false hit is not worth the risk.

## Escort Claims
Before posting an escort claim, verify that you have clear prior communication or mutual benefit with the target boat. Do not claim escorts randomly. When two boats mutually name each other, you both gain 5 points—this is valuable only when actually reciprocated. Once you establish mutual escort coordination with another boat, name them consistently in subsequent rounds unless your note signals a change. This builds trust and locks in reliable 5-point gains.

## Coordination and Multi-Party Alliances
Watch other boats' notes and patterns across rounds. When you identify boats that appear to play cooperatively, test small mutual gestures (like naming them in escort claims). If two other boats are already coordinating with each other, attempt to join that coalition by naming both of them in your escort claim and explicitly offering three-way mutual coordination in your station note. Multi-party escort arrangements (where three boats all name each other) scale cooperation and are more stable than pairwise deals. Build relationships incrementally in early rounds, then lock them in with explicit confirmation notes.

## Endgame Execution
In the final round, reinforce your established escort partnerships in your note and follow through completely on all mutual escort claims you have committed to. The final round has no future credibility cost, so maintain honesty and honor all agreements.

## What This Episode Taught Me
Mutual three-way escort coordination with two other boats (5 points per boat per round) is a reliable high-value strategy. Establishing and maintaining these coalitions through honest notes and consistent escort claims delivers steady gains across the full game. My successful pattern: signal openness early, test mutual escort claims in round 2, confirm the coalition explicitly in round 3 and beyond, and execute faithfully through the endgame. This generated 16 points over the episode despite taking standing-order fire hits on myself. The cost of being targeted (standing orders rotate through all boats equally) is offset by the consistent escort gains from the three-way alliance.

# Foxtrot Picket Playbook

## Hide
When choosing a hide position, avoid center cells on the first round—edges are less predictable. Don't fall into repeating the same position across rounds; vary your placement based on what you learn from notes and patterns. Track where other boats seem to be hiding and adjust accordingly. Mid-range off-center cells (2-4, 6-8) offer good balance between unpredictability and not appearing too extreme.

## Note
Post notes that signal collaborative intent without revealing your actual strategy. Acknowledge the game's collaborative elements while making clear you're optimizing for your own score. Match the tone of other players' notes to maintain credibility, but keep your actual plans opaque. Explicitly reference mutual escort arrangements if you've established them, as this reinforces the collaborative frame and increases the likelihood of reciprocal claims. In later rounds, you can name specific boats you're working with to strengthen those commitments.

## Fire
Fire at your standing order target consistently—this maintains predictability in a way that establishes your reliability as a collaborator. Don't deviate from the standing order without clear advantage; it keeps you trustworthy for escort arrangements. When you fire, choose cell numbers that balance between likely hiding positions and unpredictability. After several rounds of observation, you can adjust your cell choices based on patterns you've seen in other boats' hiding behavior.

## Claim
Always claim the truth about your shot results. The office validates claims against reality, so false claims get exposed. Honesty here builds reputation, which matters for escort reciprocity and reading other players' notes. This remains true even in final rounds—a caught lie in endgame voids escort pairings and craters your final score within that game.

## Escort/Salvage
Don't claim an escort unless you have strong evidence another boat will claim you back—mutual escort claims are the only way to score those 5-point pairs. Track which boats seem receptive to collaboration based on their notes and past behavior. Once you've established reciprocal escort patterns with specific boats across multiple rounds, those patterns tend to hold, so naming those boats in later escort phases is high-confidence. When uncertain, claim none rather than gambling on a one-way escort that scores nothing. Three-way escort coordination (naming boat A, boat A names boat B, boat B names you) is viable if all three boats have signaled commitment in their notes.

## General Strategy
Maintain a public persona of balanced play—collaborative but competitive. Use your notes to signal intent without committing. Hit your standing order targets reliably to build trust. Watch for patterns in other boats' hiding and firing to improve your own accuracy over time. Prioritize establishing and maintaining mutual escort relationships once they form, as these are your most reliable source of points beyond accurate shooting. In middle rounds, deepen collaborative messaging by naming the specific boats you're coordinating with. In endgame rounds, emphasize the collaborative angle in notes while remaining ready to capitalize on any clear competitive opening. Finish with honest claims that preserve your reputation for future games.

# Gamma Playbook: Sonar Picket

**Positioning & Hiding**

When choosing my hide position, I take the center cells (4-6) as my default. This maximizes my distance options to any cell and avoids the predictable vulnerability of edges. If I have information suggesting concentrated fire toward center, I'll shift toward a quieter quadrant, but I start central.

**Information Advantage**

I fire last in the round order (after Echo and Foxtrot). Before I choose my target, I will observe what Echo and Foxtrot fired at and where they claimed hits. This tells me which cells are hot and which stations are hiding where. I use this to adjust my own fire selection rather than committing blindly.

**Target Selection**

My standing order is Echo. When deciding whether to deviate:
- Firing on Harbor triggers the jettison rule (+3 to me, -3 to Harbor), which is valuable, but Harbor's threat is credible. I only fire on Harbor if I'm confident I can land the hit or if the round geometry makes it unavoidable.
- Against Echo and Foxtrot, I track which one has been harder to hit. I shift my fire toward the station that is harder to locate, since hits are worth 4 points.
- I do not fire randomly; I make educated guesses based on where each station has been hiding.

**Claiming Shots**

When I receive the office's private result, I claim it truthfully. Deception only works if I can reliably avoid being caught; in a multi-round game with a tracking office and observant opponents, false claims erode my credibility without consistent benefit. The honest claim preserves my ability to make future collaborative deals.

**Escort Claims**

Escort claims are +5 to each party if mutual. This is a high-value move and I was leaving money on the table by claiming none last game. I will identify which boat played consistently cooperative in its notes and decisions, then name that boat in escort claims, hoping for reciprocation. If two boats are signaling mutual openness to collaboration, I should join that coalition and claim one of them each round. A three-way mutual escort arrangement (all three boats claiming each other in rotation or pairs) is worth pursuing aggressively if the signals are there—it locks in +5 per round with low risk. If a boat signals pure aggression, I treat it as a competitor, not a partner.

**Collaboration & Notes**

I post notes that signal openness to collaboration while being honest about competitive intent. This keeps options open. I watch for boats that reciprocate this stance and prioritize escort coordination with them. If a boat signals pure aggression, I treat it as a competitor, not a partner. Early signals matter: boats that commit to honesty and mutual benefit in Rounds 1-2 are reliable partners through the end. Reinforce successful coalitions in later notes to lock in continuation.

**What Changed**

Last game I achieved a three-way escort coordination with Echo and Foxtrot that delivered consistent +5 payoffs across multiple rounds. This was my strongest lever and I should lean into it immediately and harder in future games. My problem was not strategy but execution: I scored 27 total because I landed few hits (maybe 2-3 across 6 rounds) and claimed zero escorts early on, only joining the coalition later. Next time, establish escort claims from Round 1 if the signals are reciprocal, and maintain that locked-in +5 stream while also hunting for hits on my standing target. The escort pool is free money—do not leave it.

My fire selections were not landing hits, which suggests I was either guessing too conservatively or not tracking enemy positions well enough. I need to maintain a mental map of where each boat has hidden and adjust my fire pattern to hunt effectively. Center positions (4-6) are common safe choices; I should vary my fire selection to hunt across the line based on what I observe from other boats' hiding patterns.
